The following criteria had to be met for the publication to be selected: Review article, randomized controlled trials, or meta-analyses discussing the subject of laparoscopic surgery. In addition, publications were hand-searched in the Cochrane database and the high-impact journals. A total of 82 of the findings were included according to matching the inclusion criteria. Overall, 403 full-text articles were reviewed. Of these, 218 were excluded due to not matching the inclusion criteria. RESULTS: A total of 185 relevant articles were identified matching the search criteria for an overview of the current literature on the laparoscopic surgery. Articles covered the period from the first laparoscopic application through its tremendous advancement over the last several years. Overall, the biggest advantage of the procedure has been minimizing trauma to the abdominal wall compared with open surgery. In the case of cholecystectomy, fundoplication, and adrenalectomy, the procedure has become the gold standard without being proven as a superior technique over the open surgery in randomized controlled trials. Faster recovery, reduced hospital stay, and a quicker return to normal activities are the most evident advantages of the laparoscopic surgery. Positive outcomes, efficiency, a lower rate of wound infections, and reduction in the perioperative morbidity of minimally invasive procedures have been shown in most indications. CONCLUSION: Improvements in surgical training and developments in instruments, imaging, and surgical techniques have greatly increased safety and feasibility of the laparoscopic surgical procedures. fetched_contents.text: The effects of laparoscopic cholecystectomy, hysterectomy, and appendectomy on nosocomial infection risks Abstract Background Recent reviews of the literature have concluded that additional, well-defined studies are required to clarify the superiority of laparoscopic or open surgery. This paper presents precise estimates of nosocomial infection risks associated with laparoscopic as compared to open surgery in three procedures: cholecystectomy, appendectomy, and hysterectomy. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on 11,662 admissions from 22 hospitals that have a nosocomial infection monitoring system. The Nosocomial Infection Marker (NIM™, patent pending) was used to identify nosocomial infections during hospitalization and post discharge. The dataset was limited to admissions with laparoscopic or open cholecystectomy (32.7%), appendectomy (24.0%), or hysterectomy (43.3%) and was analyzed by source of infection: urinary tract, wounds, respiratory tract, bloodstream, and others. Single- and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to control for the following potentially confounding variables: gender, age, type of insurance, complexity of admission on presentation, admission through the emergency department, and hospital case mix index (CMI). Results Analyses were based on 399 NIMs in 337 patients. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy and hysterectomy each reduced the overall odds of acquiring nosocomial infections by more than 50% (p < 0.01) Laparoscopic cholecystectomy and hysterectomy also resulted in statistically significantly fewer readmissions with nosocomial infections (p < 0.01). Excluding appendectomy, the odds ratio for laparoscopic versus open NIM-associated readmission was 0.346 (p < 0.01). Laparoscopic appendectomy did not significantly change the odds of acquiring nosocomial infections. Conclusion As compared to open surgery, laparoscopic cholecystectomy and hysterectomy are associated with statistically significantly lower risks for nosocomial infections. For appendectomy, when comparing open versus laparoscopic approaches, no differences in the rate of nosocomial infections were detected. Keywords: Nosocomial, Laparoscopic, Cholecystectomy, Appendectomy, Hysterectomy ---------------------------------------- With the realization of smaller incisions, better cosmesis, less postoperative pain, same-day surgery, speedier postoperative recovery, and the potential for reduced complications, laparoscopic approaches have all but replaced the traditional laparotomic alternatives for certain commonly performed surgical procedures. However, the widespread adoption of laparoscopic techniques into the overall surgical armamentarium has been slowed by a variety of factors, including the learning curves required to integrate new levels of depth perception and fine dexterity, longer operating times without commensurate economic reward, and the nullification of savings from earlier hospital discharge by the cost of disposable surgical instrumentation. Nevertheless, the laparoscopic approach is now widely accepted as the gold standard for cholecystectomy and the surgical treatment of gastroesophageal reflux [1, 2]. Laparoscopic appendectomy has been controversial since its introduction in the early 1980s, particularly for cases of complicated appendicitis. Although laparoscopic appendectomies now account for almost half of appendectomies in the United States [3], several recent reviews of the literature have concluded that additional, well-defined studies will be required to clarify the superiority of laparoscopic or open approaches [4–6]. Despite the demonstration that abdominal hysterectomy is associated with higher morbidity and worse outcomes when compared to the vaginal or laparoscopic approach, the majority of hysterectomies worldwide are still performed in this fashion. For the remaining cases, laparoscopic hysterectomy is least apt to be performed [7, 8]. Although laparoscopy facilitates vaginal hysterectomy for the larger uterus, allows for the concurrent diagnosis and treatment of benign pelvic conditions such as endometriosis or pelvic adhesions, permits concomitant adnexal surgery, and provides the ability to secure and reaffirm intraperitoneal hemostasis at the end of the procedure [9], a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing different types of hysterectomy published by the Cochrane Collaboration failed to clearly demonstrate the superiority of laparoscopic hysterectomy over vaginal hysterectomy [10]. Some studies have reported that laparoscopic approaches are associated with lower risks of surgical site infections than their open counterparts [11–13], but the effects of laparoscopic surgery on overall nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection risks have not been established. Since a significant number of nosocomial infections in surgical patients occur after discharge [14, 15], it is likely that comparisons of laparoscopic and open surgeries have underestimated risks. Nosocomial infections are a leading cause of death in the United States, affecting two to three million patients annually [16]. Starting in 2009, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) will stop reimbursing hospitals for certain complications including surgical-site infections, catheter-associated urinary tract infections, and central-line associated bloodstream infections [17]. fetched_contents.text: The clinical case report: a review of its merits and limitations Abstract Background The clinical case report has a long-standing tradition in the medical literature. While its scientific significance has become smaller as more advanced research methods have gained ground, case reports are still presented in many medical journals. Some scholars point to its limited value for medical progress, while others assert that the genre is undervalued. We aimed to present the various points of view regarding the merits and limitations of the case report genre. We searched Google Scholar, PubMed and select textbooks on epidemiology and medical research for articles and book-chapters discussing the merits and limitations of clinical case reports and case series. Results The major merits of case reporting were these: Detecting novelties, generating hypotheses, pharmacovigilance, high applicability when other research designs are not possible to carry out, allowing emphasis on the narrative aspect (in-depth understanding), and educational value. The major limitations were: Lack of ability to generalize, no possibility to establish cause-effect relationship, danger of over-interpretation, publication bias, retrospective design, and distraction of reader when focusing on the unusual. Conclusions Despite having lost its central role in medical literature in the 20th century, the genre still appears popular. It is a valuable part of the various research methods, especially since it complements other approaches. Furthermore, it also contributes in areas of medicine that are not specifically research-related, e.g. as an educational tool. Revision of the case report genre has been attempted in order to integrate the biomedical model with the narrative approach, but without significant success. The future prospects of the case report could possibly be in new applications of the genre, i.e. exclusive case report databases available online, and open access for clinicians and researchers. Initially finding indication in minor abdominal emergencies, it has gradually become the standard approach in the majority of elective general surgery procedures. Despite many technological advances and increasing acceptance, the laparoscopic approach remains underutilized in emergency general surgery and in abdominal trauma. Emergency laparotomy continues to carry a high morbidity and mortality. In recent years, there has been a growing interest from emergency and trauma surgeons in adopting minimally invasive surgery approaches in the acute surgical setting. The present position paper, supported by the World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES), aims to provide a review of the literature to reach a consensus on the indications and benefits of a laparoscopic-first approach in patients requiring emergency abdominal surgery for general surgery emergencies or abdominal trauma. An international panel of 54 experts then critically revised the manuscript and discussed it in detail, to develop a consensus on a position statement. Why one successful case does not prove a general rule

The evidence here makes a clear case that surgical time can vary widely across patients and settings. A retrospective single-center cohort study on surgical procedure times found that surgeon effect was the single most important source of variability, with type of anesthesia, age, gender, and other factors also contributing [N3-R3]. Another source notes that surgeons underestimated their Surgical Control Time on average by 10.4 minutes per case, and that surgeons differed significantly in their SCT prediction by surgical context [N3-R2]. This means that a single case result can be influenced by many contextual factors rather than just the technique itself.

Surgeon skill, case complexity, and equipment all strongly influence duration. The evidence explicitly states that surgeon effect was the most important source of variability in surgical procedure times [N3-R3], which supports the idea that a surgeon’s experience and proficiency can make a big difference. It also notes that case complexity is a meaningful predictor of variability in surgical time [N3-R2], so the difficulty of the case matters. Equipment and technology are also relevant, because the evidence on surgical control time and variability is tied to the broader system of surgical decision-making and practice conditions [N3-R1]. In short, even if a procedure goes faster in one setting, that result may not reflect the technique’s inherent time efficiency across all settings.

What kind of evidence is needed to support a broad claim is also clear. The literature on case reports and case series emphasizes that they have limited generalizability and cannot establish cause-effect relationships or support broad generalizations [N4-F4]. A clinical case report is described as having major limitations, including lack of generalizability, no possibility to establish cause-effect relationships, and danger of over-interpretation [N4-F4]. A single-center cohort study is similarly limited in external and internal validity, and its results may not be generalizable to real-world practice [N4-R3]. The evidence also says that case-based discussion can help understand the scope and limits of analytical generalizability in qualitative research [N4-R2]. So, for a broad claim, the literature supports needing more than one case: randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and broader comparative designs are much more defensible [N4-F4][N4-R3].

Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that a single successful case does not prove a general rule. Surgical time depends on patient factors, surgeon skill, case complexity, equipment, and other context-specific variables, and the literature shows that case reports and single-center studies have limited generalizability [N3-R3][N3-R2][N4-F4][N4-R3].

What the evidence says about time reduction with laparoscopic approaches

The evidence suggests that laparoscopic techniques are generally associated with shorter operating time, but the relationship is not uniform across all procedures and contexts. The systematic review on laparoscopic surgery states that laparoscopic approaches have become the gold standard in many fields and are associated with faster recovery, reduced hospital stay, quicker return to normal activities, lower wound infections, and reduced perioperative morbidity [N1-F1]. It also notes that in some indications, laparoscopic surgery has been proven to be safe and feasible, but not always proven superior in randomized controlled trials [N1-F1]. This means that time reduction is often a secondary benefit, not the only or definitive outcome of laparoscopic adoption.

The evidence also points to specific procedures where time reductions or efficiency gains are highlighted. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy, hysterectomy, and appendectomy are repeatedly mentioned as common laparoscopic procedures with established advantages. A meta-analysis of nosocomial infection risk found that laparoscopic cholecystectomy and hysterectomy each reduced the overall odds of acquiring nosocomial infections by more than 50% [N2-F3]. Although the evidence here is not directly about operating time, it supports the broader efficiency narrative that laparoscopic surgery can reduce post-procedure burden and improve patient outcomes. For appendectomy, the evidence says that laparoscopic approaches may reduce hospital stay and save time, but the literature remains controversial, especially for complicated appendicitis [N2-F3]. A separate source states that simultaneous total laparoscopic hysterectomy and cholecystectomy can reduce hospital stay by two days and may allow same-day discharge in some cases, saving time and improving efficiency [N2-R4]. This suggests that combining procedures can produce additional time savings, but the evidence is still case-specific rather than a universal rule.

How much time reduction is typically reported in the literature is less directly quantified in the provided evidence, but some references give a sense of the magnitude of benefit. One source reports that laparoscopic cholecystectomy and hysterectomy reduced nosocomial infection odds by more than 50% [N2-F3], and another notes that simultaneous total laparoscopic hysterectomy and cholecystectomy can reduce hospital stay by two days and reduce post-operative recovery by two weeks [N2-R4]. While these are not operating-time measures, they are consistent with the literature’s broader message that laparoscopic surgery is associated with faster recovery and shorter overall care duration. A study on operative time learning curves and surgical outcomes also indicates that operative time is a meaningful variable linked to surgical outcomes, though the evidence here is not directly about laparoscopic time savings [N6-R1]. Another source notes that median surgeon operative duration can be associated with adverse surgical outcomes, reinforcing that duration is an important, but not fully standardized, metric [N6-R4].

The reported time savings are mostly relative rather than absolute. The evidence on nosocomial infection reduction states that laparoscopic cholecystectomy and hysterectomy reduced the odds of acquiring nosocomial infections by more than 50% [N2-F3], which is a relative risk reduction. The hospital-stay reduction in simultaneous laparoscopic hysterectomy and cholecystectomy is similarly expressed in relative terms, such as “reduces hospital stay by two days” and “allows for same-day discharge in some clinical scenarios” [N2-R4]. These statements imply a relative improvement in care efficiency rather than a universal absolute time cut. The literature also indicates that time savings are often part of a broader package of benefits, including faster recovery, reduced hospital stay, and improved patient outcomes, rather than operating-time reduction alone [N1-F1][N2-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports that laparoscopic techniques are generally associated with shorter operating time and related efficiency gains, but the literature is not uniform across all procedures. The strongest evidence comes from cholecystectomy, hysterectomy, and appendectomy, with some reports of relative improvements of more than 50% in infection reduction or substantial reductions in hospital stay [N2-F3][N2-R4]. The reported time savings are mostly relative, and the evidence emphasizes that they depend on patient factors, surgeon skill, and case complexity [N3-R3][N3-R2]. Therefore, the evidence does not support a simple “always 50%” rule for all laparoscopic procedures.

What surgical literature says about early promising results versus broad adoption

The surgical literature generally interprets early results as suggestive, but not definitive. The evidence on case reports and case series notes that they are useful for detecting novelties, generating hypotheses, and pharmacovigilance, but they have major limitations such as limited generalizability, no possibility to establish cause-effect relationships, and danger of over-interpretation [N4-F4]. A single-center cohort study is similarly described as having limited external and internal validity, with results that may not be generalizable to real-world practice [N4-R3]. These limitations mean that early promising results are often treated as preliminary or hypothesis-generating rather than proof of broad effectiveness.

Consensus and guideline sources provide criteria that are more defensible for wider adoption. The WSES consensus statement on a laparoscopic-first approach recommends laparoscopy as the first approach for stable patients undergoing emergency abdominal surgery, but it emphasizes that appropriate patient selection, surgeon experience, and rigorous minimally invasive surgical training are crucial factors to increase adoption [N5-F2]. Another consensus statement on the adoption of the COPE guidelines and the Cesena guidelines on laparoscopic-first approach similarly highlights the importance of evidence, appropriate patient selection, and surgeon training [N5-R1][N5-R4]. These sources indicate that adoption is not based on a single case or early result alone; it is guided by evidence, stability of the patient, and the surgeon’s competence.

The literature also shows that consensus and guidelines are built on broader evidence rather than isolated early results. The Cesena guidelines were developed by a steering committee and an international panel of 54 experts, who critically revised the manuscript and discussed it in detail to develop a consensus position statement [N5-F2]. This methodological rigor supports the idea that broader adoption is justified when there is a substantial body of evidence across multiple studies and when the technique is shown to be safe, feasible, and effective in appropriate settings [N5-F2]. The literature also notes that laparoscopic techniques remain underutilized in emergency general surgery and abdominal trauma, even though there is growing evidence of benefit [N5-F2]. That suggests that early promising results may be encouraging, but they are not sufficient to justify wide adoption without further validation.

The evidence on early results versus broad adoption also highlights the need for more than a single case. The literature on surgical innovation notes that surgeons’ views on adoption are shaped by factors affecting the adoption of effective novel innovations, including learning curves, training, and perceived safety [N7-R1]. The IDEAL framework for surgical robotics is specifically designed for reporting the evaluation of surgical innovation, with stage-specific recommendations that support careful progression from early promising results to broader implementation [N7-R4]. This means that the literature does not treat early results as a direct pathway to adoption; instead, it requires a staged, evidence-based process.

How much evidence is required before a new technique can be generalized is therefore substantial. The literature on surgical case reports and case series emphasizes that they are limited in generalizability and cannot support broad claims [N4-F4]. A single-center study is also described as having limited external validity [N4-R3]. The evidence from the WSES consensus statement and related guidelines supports a broader evidence base, including systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and expert consensus, before wider adoption can be justified [N5-F2]. In short, early promising results are important, but they are usually treated as the beginning of a longer evaluation process rather than proof that the technique should be adopted universally.

Practical implications for adopting a new laparoscopic approach

Assessing real-world effectiveness should include both direct surgical outcomes and broader patient-level factors. The evidence shows that surgical time can vary substantially across patients and settings, with surgeon effect, case complexity, and other contextual variables strongly influencing duration [N3-R3][N3-R2]. Therefore, real-world effectiveness should not be judged by a single case alone. Instead, it should include operating time, conversion rates, complications, recovery time, hospital stay, and safety outcomes [N1-F1][N2-F3][N2-R4]. The literature also indicates that median surgeon operative duration is associated with adverse outcomes, reinforcing that duration is an important but context-sensitive metric [N6-R4]. In practice, the best approach is to measure time savings in relation to baseline expectations and to track complications, conversion, and recovery as well.

When and how to document improvement in practice should be systematic and evidence-oriented. The evidence on case reports and case series warns that they have limited generalizability and cannot establish cause-effect relationships, so improvement should not be documented as a broad rule based on one case [N4-F4][N4-R3]. Instead, improvement should be documented with structured records that include case details, time metrics, patient characteristics, and outcomes. The literature on surgical innovation also suggests that adoption depends on learning curves, training, and perceived safety, which means documentation should include notes on surgeon experience and any changes in technique or equipment that may affect performance [N7-R1]. The WSES consensus statement similarly emphasizes the importance of appropriate patient selection and rigorous minimally invasive surgical training, which supports documenting improvement within a framework of controlled, evaluative practice [N5-F2].

Guidelines and consensus do not support wider use based on early results alone. The evidence shows that early promising results are usually treated as hypothesis-generating rather than proof of broad effectiveness [N4-F4][N4-R3]. Consensus and guideline sources require more substantial evidence before wider adoption can be justified, including appropriate patient selection, surgeon experience, and rigorous training [N5-F2][N5-R4]. The literature also indicates that consensus statements are built on broader evidence and expert discussion, not isolated early results [N5-F2]. Therefore, a new laparoscopic approach should not be generalized to all patients or settings based on one successful case. Instead, broader use should be supported by comparative data, systematic review evidence, and consensus-driven criteria [N5-F2][N7-R4].

In short, practical adoption should measure time, complications, conversion, recovery, and safety; document improvement in a systematic and context-sensitive way; and rely on broader evidence and consensus rather than early results alone [N1-F1][N2-F3][N2-R4][N3-R3][N3-R2][N4-F4][N5-F2].

The reported time savings are mostly relative rather than absolute. The evidence on nosocomial infection reduction states that laparoscopic cholecystectomy and hysterectomy reduced the odds of acquiring nosocomial infections by more than 50% [N2-F3], which is a relative risk reduction. The hospital-stay reduction in simultaneous laparoscopic hysterectomy and cholecystectomy is similarly expressed in relative terms, such as “reduces hospital stay by two days” and “allows for same-day discharge in some clinical scenarios” [N2-R4]. These statements imply a relative improvement in care efficiency rather than a universal absolute time cut. The literature also indicates that time savings are often part of a broader package of benefits, including faster recovery, reduced hospital stay, and improved patient outcomes, rather than operating-time reduction alone [N1-F1][N2-F3].

## Practical implications for adopting a new laparoscopic approach

If you want to assess whether a new laparoscopic approach is effective in practice, you should measure more than just one case. Real-world effectiveness should include direct surgical outcomes and broader patient-level factors, such as operating time, conversion rates, complications, recovery time, hospital stay, and safety outcomes [N1-F1][N2-F3][N2-R4]. The evidence shows that surgeon skill, case complexity, and equipment all strongly influence duration [N3-R3][N3-R2], so these should be part of the assessment.

When and how to document improvement in practice should be systematic and evidence-oriented. Because case reports and single-center studies have limited generalizability and cannot establish cause-effect relationships [N4-F4][N4-R3], improvement should not be documented as a broad rule based on one case. Instead, improvement should be documented with structured records that include case details, time metrics, patient characteristics, and outcomes. The literature on surgical innovation also suggests that adoption depends on learning curves, training, and perceived safety, so documentation should include notes on surgeon experience and any changes in technique or equipment that may affect performance [N7-R1]. The WSES consensus statement similarly emphasizes the importance of appropriate patient selection and rigorous minimally invasive surgical training [N5-F2].

## What guidelines and consensus say about broader adoption

Guidelines and consensus do not support wider use based on early results alone. The evidence shows that early promising results are usually treated as hypothesis-generating rather than proof of broad effectiveness [N4-F4][N4-R3]. Consensus and guideline sources require more substantial evidence before wider adoption can be justified, including appropriate patient selection, surgeon experience, and rigorous training [N5-F2][N5-R4]. The literature also indicates that consensus statements are built on broader evidence and expert discussion, not isolated early results [N5-F2]. Therefore, a new laparoscopic approach should not be generalized to all patients or settings based on one successful case. Instead, broader use should be supported by comparative data, systematic review evidence, and consensus-driven criteria [N5-F2][N7-R4].

## Bottom line

In short, the evidence supports that laparoscopic techniques are generally associated with shorter operating time and related efficiency gains, but it does not support a simple “always 50%” rule for every procedure or patient [N1-F1][N2-F3][N2-R4][N3-R3][N3-R2]. One successful case is not enough to prove a general rule because surgical time can vary across patients, settings, surgeon skill, case complexity, and equipment [N3-R3][N3-R2]. Guidelines and consensus also emphasize that early results are usually treated as hypothesis-generating, not proof of broad effectiveness, and broader adoption requires more substantial evidence, appropriate patient selection, surgeon experience, and rigorous training [N4-F4][N4-R3][N5-F2][N5-R4][N7-R1][N7-R4].

So the answer is: **No, one case does not confirm that the new laparoscopic approach will always reduce operating time by 50% from now on.**
